analysis.one_liner: Requires online platforms to disclose their algorithms, test them for discrimination, and open ads and moderation to public inspection.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from July 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required commercial online platforms like social networks to explain in plain language what personal data their algorithms use and how they rank content, keep records testing whether those algorithms produce unequal outcomes by race, sex, disability, and other traits, and publish annual reports on their content moderation and a public library of their advertisements. It would make it illegal for a platform's algorithms to discriminate in housing, jobs, credit, insurance, healthcare, or education, or to be used to deceive voters about how or when to vote. Users could sue for violations, the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, and a federal task force would study discriminatory uses of personal data.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary users of social media and other online platforms, especially members of groups that have documented how ad-targeting and recommendation systems can steer housing, job, credit, and other opportunities away from them. Whistleblowers inside platforms and users who want to move their data to a competitor also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social media users, especially marginalized groups

how_it_helps.text: Platforms would have to explain in plain language, in every language they serve, what personal information their algorithms collect and how that data is used to amplify or withhold content [S2][S3].

Large platforms would have to assess and document whether their algorithms produce unequal outcomes by race, sex, disability, and other traits, and keep those records for five years for regulators to inspect [S3].

It would become unlawful for a platform's design or algorithms to discriminate in housing, employment, credit, insurance, healthcare, or education, or to process personal information in a way that deceives or intimidates voters [S3].
Platforms would have to publish annual content moderation transparency reports and maintain a public, searchable library of advertisements, including who paid and how ads were targeted [S3].
Users could sue for $2,500 or actual damages, and state attorneys general and the FTC could enforce the rules; the bill also bars forced arbitration of these rights and protects whistleblowers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms and the digital advertising business built on their data. They would face disclosure, record-keeping, testing, and certification costs, legal exposure to user lawsuits, and constraints on how they target ads and rank content.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and advertising platforms

drawbacks.text: The 'safe and effective' standard for algorithms is vague, and platforms argued-style concerns that it could force changes to ranking systems whose effects are hard to predict, or chill lawful personalization [S3].

The private right of action with a $2,500 minimum statutory payout per violation could generate heavy litigation against platforms, costs that are likely to be passed on to users and advertisers [S3].

Publishing detailed content-moderation transparency reports, including counts of government takedown requests, can itself become a political target — lawmakers of both parties have at times pressured platforms over moderation decisions, and standardized public reports give them new material to cite [S3].

Even with a small-business exemption (under $25 million in revenue, under 100,000 users, under 50 workers), mid-sized platforms and startups above that line would face substantial compliance and record-retention costs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer and civil-rights benefits are real but untested: algorithmic discrimination in housing, jobs, and credit is documented, and the bill's transparency and enforcement tools directly target it. The costs fall almost entirely on the platforms themselves, though some could reach users through litigation exposure and compliance-driven changes. The bill's most contested feature is the vague 'safe and effective' mandate combined with broad private lawsuits, which courts and regulators would have spent years defining.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications and Technology subcommittee in July 2023, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Doris Matsui introduced the bill on July 13, 2023, with Representative Kweisi Mfume as an original cosponsor [S1][S3].

It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on July 13, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology the next day; the action history shows no further activity [S5].
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee, so it died without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online platforms and the targeted-advertising business avoided new disclosure, record-keeping, antidiscrimination, and lawsuit exposure that would have applied to their algorithms. No one else gained anything from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and ad platforms

for.name: Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 14 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all of its cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Cathy McMorris Rodgers (R-WA) in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill in committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republicans signed on; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican, and there were no roll-call votes on the bill.

industries.industry: Social media and large online platforms
industries.note: They would have had to disclose how their algorithms use personal data, keep five-year records of fairness testing, publish moderation reports, certify compliance under oath, and face user lawsuits for discriminatory algorithms. Their current business model of opaque ranking and targeting is exactly what the bill targeted.

Ad libraries, targeting disclosures, and FTC rules against deceptive and discriminatory advertising would constrain targeted ad sales, especially in housing, jobs, credit, and insurance where discriminatory targeting is documented. Some advertisers benefit from a more verifiable marketplace, but the targeting practices at the core of the industry lose.

Platforms under $25 million in revenue, 100,000 users, and 50 workers were exempt from most requirements, sparing them compliance costs, but any startup growing past those thresholds would inherit the full burden.
